title: Introduction to lidR for Forest Inventory
text:
About lidR
lidR is an open-source R package for analyzing airborne LiDAR point clouds, creating raster products, and extracting forest structure information. The pages in this section focus on its applications to forest inventory. The package was developed at Université Laval in Québec, Canada, and is maintained by Jean-Romain Roussel. The current release is available on CRAN, and its source code is hosted on GitHub.

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text: This tutorial demonstrates how to convert field plot coordinates into a spatial dataset and derive plot-level forest inventory attributes from individual-tree measurements using R. It follows the workflow in plot_generation.R, including coordinate transformation, tree biomass and volume estimation, plot summaries, and spatial data export.

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text:
Relevant Resources
The workflow uses the sf, dplyr, and readr R packages. For additional information, see the sf documentation, dplyr documentation, and readr documentation.

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text:
Dataset Background
The example in plot_generation.R uses a CSV named 2026_Nahanni_LiDAR_Calibration_Plots.csv. This file supplies plot coordinates and individual-tree records, including plot identifiers, species, diameter at breast height (DBH), and tree height. The script uses the same CSV for both plot locations and tree measurements, although the functions also accept separate CSV files.

Summary of Processing Steps

Install and load required R packages.
Define species-specific volume and biomass coefficients.
Calculate above-ground biomass and stem volume for individual trees.
Convert plot coordinates from a CSV to spatial points and transform their coordinate reference system.
Summarize tree measurements and calculated attributes by plot.
Join the summaries to the plot locations and export shapefiles.

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text:
2) Volume and Biomass Coefficients
Species-specific allometric equations are used to estimate tree volume and above-ground biomass from DBH and height.

Tree volume
The volume equation is:
\[
V = b_0 + b_1 \times DBH^{b_2} \times H^{b_3}
\]
where \(V\) is tree volume in cubic metres, \(DBH\) is diameter at breast height in centimetres, \(H\) is tree height in metres, and \(b_0\)–\(b_3\) are coefficients selected by species.


Above-ground biomass
Above-ground biomass is calculated separately for wood, bark, branches, and foliage:
\[
AGB_c = b_1 \times DBH^{b_2} \times H^{b_3}
\]
The total tree above-ground biomass is the sum of the four components:
\[
AGB_{tree} = AGB_{wood} + AGB_{bark} + AGB_{branches} + AGB_{foliage}
\]
The coefficients below are taken directly from plot_generation.R. They include species-specific and broader softwood/hardwood groups. The script does not automatically assign an unmatched species to a broader group; the species value must match an available coefficient name.

section: 4) Convert Plot Coordinates to Spatial Points
text:
4) Convert Plot Coordinates to Spatial Points
The csv_to_shp() function reads plot coordinates from a CSV, verifies the required columns, and creates an sf point layer.
If a plot identifier is provided, records with the same plot ID are grouped and their mean longitude and latitude are used to create a single point. The coordinates are then transformed from the input CRS to the output CRS and saved as an ESRI Shapefile.






Note



The script averages duplicate coordinates in the input coordinate system before transforming them. This is intended for repeated records representing the same plot, rather than distinct sampling locations.




Code
csv_to_shp <- function(
    csv_path,                  # Path to the input CSV containing coordinates
    output_shp,                # Path for the output shapefile
    x_col = "longitude",       # Name of the x-coordinate column
    y_col = "latitude",        # Name of the y-coordinate column
    plot_id = NULL,            # Optional plot ID column used to group duplicate plots
    input_crs,                 # CRS of the coordinates in the CSV
    output_crs                 # CRS for the output spatial layer
) {

  # Read the CSV file
  df <- readr::read_csv(
    csv_path,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  # Check that the coordinate columns exist
  required <- c(x_col, y_col)

  # If a plot ID is provided, also check that it exists
  if (!is.null(plot_id)) {
    required <- c(required, plot_id)
  }

  missing <- setdiff(required, names(df))

  # Stop if any required columns are missing
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop(
      paste0(
        "Missing required columns: ",
        paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
        "\nCheck that x_col = '", x_col,
        "' and y_col = '", y_col, "'",
        if (!is.null(plot_id)) {
          paste0(" and plot_id = '", plot_id, "'")
        } else {
          ""
        },
        " match the column names in the CSV."
      )
    )
  }

  # If a plot ID column is supplied, group duplicate plot IDs
  # and calculate the mean x and y coordinates for each plot
  if (!is.null(plot_id)) {

    df <- df |>
      dplyr::group_by(.data[[plot_id]]) |>
      dplyr::summarise(
        "{x_col}" := mean(.data[[x_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
        "{y_col}" := mean(.data[[y_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      )
  }

  # Convert the data frame to an sf spatial point layer
  out <- sf::st_as_sf(
    df,
    coords = c(x_col, y_col),
    crs = input_crs,
    remove = FALSE
  )

  # Transform the points to the desired output CRS
  out <- sf::st_transform(
    out,
    crs = output_crs
  )

  # Save the spatial layer as an ESRI Shapefile
  sf::st_write(
    out,
    output_shp,
    driver = "ESRI Shapefile",
    delete_layer = TRUE,
    quiet = TRUE
  )

  # Return the spatial layer for continued use in R
  return(out)
}

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text:
5) Summarize Individual-Tree Measurements by Plot
The summarize_plots() function reads the tree CSV, checks the required fields, and standardizes species code capitalization (for example, SW or sw becomes Sw).
It then calculates biomass and volume for every tree before grouping the records by plot ID. For each plot, the script calculates:

Number of recorded trees (n_trees)
Mean, minimum, and maximum DBH (dbh_mean, dbh_min, dbh_max)
Mean, minimum, and maximum height (ht_mean, ht_min, ht_max)
Tree density in trees per hectare (density_tpha)
Above-ground biomass in tonnes per hectare (agb_t_ha)
Volume in cubic metres per hectare (vlm_m3_ha)


Convert totals to per-hectare estimates
With plot area \(A\) expressed in hectares, the conversions are:
\[
Density = \frac{n_{trees}}{A}
\]
\[
AGB_{t/ha} = \frac{AGB_{kg}}{1000 \times A}
\]
\[
Volume_{m^3/ha} = \frac{Volume_{m^3}}{A}
\]
For the example 400 m² plots, \(A = 0.04\) ha.






Note



The script counts all records in n_trees, uses na.rm = TRUE when summarizing measurements and calculated biomass/volume, and does not include a separate quality-control or missing-data filtering stage. Review the input measurements and species codes before interpreting the resulting estimates.




Code
summarize_plots <- function(
    tree_csv,                  # Path to CSV containing individual tree records
    plot_id = "nfm_id",        # Column identifying the plot for each tree
    dbh_col = "dbh",           # Column containing DBH measurements
    height_col = "height",     # Column containing tree height measurements
    species_col = "species",   # Column containing species information
    plot_area_ha = 0.04        # Plot area in hectares
) {

  # Read the individual tree data
  trees <- readr::read_csv(
    tree_csv,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  # Check that all required columns exist in the tree data
  required <- c(
    plot_id,
    dbh_col,
    height_col,
    species_col
  )

  missing <- setdiff(required, names(trees))

  # Stop if any required columns are missing
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop(
      paste0(
        "Missing required columns: ",
        paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
        "\nCheck that plot_id = '", plot_id,
        "', dbh_col = '", dbh_col,
        "', height_col = '", height_col,
        "', and species_col = '", species_col,
        "' match the column names in the CSV."
      )
    )
  }


  # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Standardize species codes
  # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  #
  # Converts species codes to consistent capitalization so that
  # differences in capitalization do not affect coefficient matching.
  #
  # Examples:
  #   "SW" -> "Sw"
  #   "sw" -> "Sw"
  #   "PL" -> "Pl"
  #   "AT" -> "At"
  #

  trees <- trees |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      "{species_col}" := paste0(
        toupper(substr(.data[[species_col]], 1, 1)),
        tolower(substr(
          .data[[species_col]],
          2,
          nchar(.data[[species_col]])
        ))
      )
    )


  # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Calculate biomass and volume for each individual tree
  # -----------------------------------------------------------------------

  trees <- trees |>
    dplyr::rowwise() |>
    dplyr::mutate(

      # Above-ground biomass in kilograms
      AGB_kg = calc_agb(
        species = .data[[species_col]],
        dbh = .data[[dbh_col]],
        height = .data[[height_col]]
      ),

      # Tree volume in cubic metres
      Volume_m3 = calc_volume(
        species = .data[[species_col]],
        dbh = .data[[dbh_col]],
        height = .data[[height_col]]
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::ungroup()


  # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Group trees by plot and calculate plot-level summaries
  # -----------------------------------------------------------------------

  summary <- trees |>

    # Group all trees belonging to the same plot
    dplyr::group_by(.data[[plot_id]]) |>

    # Calculate summary statistics for each plot
    dplyr::summarise(

      # Number of trees measured in the plot
      n_trees = dplyr::n(),

      # DBH summary statistics
      dbh_mean = mean(.data[[dbh_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      dbh_min  = min(.data[[dbh_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      dbh_max  = max(.data[[dbh_col]], na.rm = TRUE),

      # Height summary statistics
      ht_mean = mean(.data[[height_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      ht_min  = min(.data[[height_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      ht_max  = max(.data[[height_col]], na.rm = TRUE),

      # Total above-ground biomass in the plot (kg)
      agb_kg = sum(
        AGB_kg,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

      # Total tree volume in the plot (m3)
      volume_m3 = sum(
        Volume_m3,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

      # Remove grouping after summarising
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Convert plot-level totals to per-hectare values
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------

    dplyr::mutate(

      # Trees per hectare
      density_tpha =
        n_trees / plot_area_ha,

      # Above-ground biomass in tonnes per hectare
      agb_t_ha =
        (agb_kg / 1000) /
        plot_area_ha,

      # Volume in cubic metres per hectare
      vlm_m3_ha =
        volume_m3 /
        plot_area_ha
    ) |>

    # Remove intermediate plot totals
    dplyr::select(
      -agb_kg,
      -volume_m3
    )

  # Return one row per plot containing the calculated summaries
  return(summary)
}

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text:
6) Filepaths and User Inputs
Update the filepaths, field names, coordinate reference systems, and plot area for your dataset.
The example uses:

Input CRS: EPSG:4326 (WGS 84 longitude/latitude)
Output CRS: EPSG:32608 (WGS 84 / UTM Zone 8N)
Plot area: 0.04 ha (400 m²)

The script creates an intermediate plot-location shapefile (plots.shp) and a final shapefile with tree summaries (plots_summary.shp).

plot_csv <- "F:\\yukon\\plot_generation\\2026_Nahanni_LiDAR_Calibration_Plots.csv"

# Tree CSV containing individual tree measurements
tree_csv <- "F:\\yukon\\plot_generation\\2026_Nahanni_LiDAR_Calibration_Plots.csv"

# Intermediate shapefile containing only plot locations
plot_shp <- "F:\\yukon\\plot_generation\\plots.shp"

# Final shapefile containing plot locations + tree summaries
output_shp <- "F:\\yukon\\plot_generation\\plots_summary.shp"


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Column names
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Coordinate columns
x_col <- "Longitude"
y_col <- "Latitude"

# Column identifying each plot
plot_id <- "Plot ID"

# Individual tree columns
dbh_col <- "DBH (cm)"
height_col <- "Height (m)"

# Species column
#
# Values in this column must correspond to names in the biomass
# and volume coefficient lists (e.g., Sw, Sb, At, Pl, Bw).
species_col <- "Species"


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Coordinate reference systems
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# EPSG:4326 = WGS84 latitude/longitude
# EPSG:32608 = WGS84 / UTM Zone 8N
#

input_crs <- 4326
output_crs <- 32608


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Plot area in hectares
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# 400 m2 plot = 0.04 ha
#

plot_area_ha <- 0.04

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text:
7) Run the Plot Generation Workflow

Create the spatial plot layer
First, convert the CSV coordinates to a spatial point layer. Duplicate records sharing a plot ID are represented by one point using their mean coordinates.

plots <- csv_to_shp(
  csv_path = plot_csv,
  output_shp = plot_shp,
  x_col = x_col,
  y_col = y_col,
  plot_id = plot_id,
  input_crs = input_crs,
  output_crs = output_crs
)



Calculate plot-level attributes
Next, calculate individual-tree biomass and volume and aggregate the results by plot.

plot_summary <- summarize_plots(
  tree_csv = tree_csv,
  plot_id = plot_id,
  dbh_col = dbh_col,
  height_col = height_col,
  species_col = species_col,
  plot_area_ha = plot_area_ha
)



Join plot attributes to spatial locations
The summaries are joined to the spatial point layer using the plot identifier. The left_join() retains the spatial plot records even if no matching tree summary is found.

plots_summary <- plots |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    plot_summary,
    by = plot_id
  )



Export the final shapefile
Save the spatial layer with its plot-level attributes. The existing output layer is replaced when the script is rerun.

sf::st_write(
  plots_summary,
  output_shp,
  driver = "ESRI Shapefile",
  delete_layer = TRUE,
  quiet = TRUE
)



Inspect the results
Print the final spatial layer to inspect the attributes and geometry.

print(plots_summary)

title: Plot Generation and Tree Summaries
text:
8) Outputs
The workflow produces two spatial datasets:







Output
Description




plots.shp
One spatial point per plot, derived from the CSV coordinates


plots_summary.shp
Spatial plot points joined to DBH, height, tree count, density, biomass, and volume summaries



Both outputs are ESRI Shapefiles. Shapefile attribute names may be shortened because of format limitations; check the exported field names when using the results in subsequent analyses.
The resulting plot-level dataset can be used as reference data for subsequent forest inventory and remote sensing analyses.

title: Multi-Scale Biomass Mapping and Timber Assessment in the Yukon Territory
text:
Overview
This website is a central resource for the Multi-Scale Biomass Mapping and Timber Assessment in the Yukon Territory project, undertaken in collaboration with the Yukon Government and the University of British Columbia’s Integrated Remote Sensing Studio. It provides tutorials for processing and analysing forest inventory and remote sensing data, alongside practical examples of methods and outputs developed through the project’s work packages.
The project integrates field measurements, satellite imagery, environmental datasets, airborne LiDAR, and drone-based remote sensing to support forest biomass estimation, enhanced forest inventories, and post-fire assessment. The tutorials and examples are intended to document reproducible workflows and support their application to Yukon forest management and planning.

title: Multi-Scale Biomass Mapping and Timber Assessment in the Yukon Territory
text:
Project work packages
The project includes complementary postdoctoral and PhD research components.

Postdoctoral Research: Multiscale Forest Biomass and Inventory Assessment
This research focuses on developing a multiscale remote sensing framework that integrates satellite imagery, airborne and drone-based LiDAR, and field observations to improve forest biomass estimation and inventory assessments across Yukon. Through three interconnected work packages, the project aims to provide reliable, spatially explicit information to support carbon accounting, wildfire planning, timber salvage, and sustainable forest management, while developing reproducible workflows for operational use. The work is organized into three work packages:

Work Package 1: Territory-wide biomass mapping
Develop a territory-wide forest biomass map using field plot measurements, satellite imagery, topographic and climate information, and predictive modelling. Project resources will cover data preparation, biomass estimation, model validation, uncertainty assessment, and mapping.


Work Package 2: Rapid Enhanced Forest Inventory
Develop reproducible LiDAR-based workflows for generating forest inventory attributes at finer spatial scales, including approaches that can support assessment of fire-affected forests. Resources will include point-cloud processing, structural metric generation, inventory modelling, and example mapping outputs.


Work Package 3: Post-fire stand inventory and assessment
Evaluate drone-based LiDAR and imagery for characterizing post-fire forest conditions and supporting inventory and salvage planning. Examples will illustrate data acquisition and processing approaches, comparison with field measurements, and assessment of forest structural attributes.



PhD Research: Multi-Platform LiDAR Quantification of Post-Fire Slash Biomass and Integration into Carbon Accounting and Wildfire Risk Systems in Yukon Boreal Forests
The PhD component focuses on quantifying slash pile biomass using multiple LiDAR platforms and integrating post-fire structural information into carbon accounting and wildfire risk assessment. The work is organized into two work packages:

Work Package 1: Multi-Platform Data Acquisition and Structural Assessment
Establish representative fire- and harvest-affected study sites across Yukon to evaluate the use of drone LiDAR, airborne LiDAR, and photogrammetry for characterizing slash piles. Ground measurements and three-dimensional point cloud metrics will be used to assess pile structure, volume, and variability across different forest and environmental conditions.


Work Package 2: Biomass Estimation and Cross-Platform Transferability
Develop and evaluate statistical and machine learning models to estimate slash pile biomass from remotely sensed structural metrics. This work will assess model accuracy, uncertainty, and transferability across LiDAR platforms, with the goal of establishing reproducible workflows and operational guidelines for biomass estimation in Yukon forests.

title: Multi-Scale Biomass Mapping and Timber Assessment in the Yukon Territory
text:

Tutorials and worked examples will be added as project workflows and datasets become available.

Learn how to generate spatially distributed sample plots for forest inventory and biomass modelling. This tutorial covers plot placement, sampling considerations, and the creation of geospatial plot datasets for subsequent analysis. Open the plot generation tutorial.
